41949.etyen:
Borrowed from Middle Low German oldevater (“father of the parents; grandfather”), alongside oldervater (“father of the parents; grandfather”). The second element was adapted to Norwegian far (“father”), while the first element became the kinship prefix olde-. The Middle Low German term originally denoted a grandfather; in Norwegian, the meaning later shifted one generation further back to “great-grandfather”.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk oldefar and Danish oldefar (“great-grandfather”). See also oldemor (“great-grandmother”).

1005021.etyen:
From remisere (“to draw, tie a chess game”) + -ing (“action/result-forming noun suffix”).
The base remisere (“to draw, tie a chess game”) is derived from remis (“draw, tie”), ultimately from French remis (“put back, reset”), the masculine singular past participle of remettre (“to put back, reset”), from Latin remittō (“send back; let go; remit”). Remittō contains mittō (“send, let go”), probably from Proto-Italic *meitō (“send, put forth”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“change, exchange; remove, send”).
